transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (CTO, Orchid), Sara (ML Eng), Luis (Infra)
Links referenced: /redwood/security-pack.pdf, internal-benchmark-template.xlsx, deck: hosted-vs-dedicated.pdf

[00:00] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining us, appreciate the time. Quick intro, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE. Priya is our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Mark: Good, thanks. we've got about an hour, so we'll go through where we are.
[00:12] Sara: Hi, I'm Sara, I'm the ML engineer running our chat pipelines, mostly using OpenAI right now via Azure.
[00:18] Luis: Luis here, infra lead, I'll ask the security questions.
[00:22] Priya: Awesome. Quick agenda — 1) understand current stack and pain points, 2) discuss migration paths (hosted, dedicated, private), 3) parity and benchmarks, 4) next steps. Sound good?
[00:30] Mark: Yep. We can kick off.

[00:45] Sara: So high level — we've been on Azure OpenAI for the past year, primary models for chat + embeddings. Latency is fine most times but cost has crept up. We're also experimenting w/ vLLM on prem for a couple of internal tooling use cases; TGI-based inference for a retriever-ranker flow. We're worried about parity if we move providers and also about the ops overhead of maintaining vLLM clusters.
[01:10] Alex: Totally — that's a pretty common pattern. When you say parity what are the exact metrics y'all care about? Latency, BLEU-ish? token-level quality?
[01:20] Sara: Mainly p50/p95 latency end-to-end, token cost, and then a small set of regression prompts where we need identical or better behavior — basically eval parity across prompt suite.
[01:32] Priya: Helpful, and what's your traffic profile? bursts or steady?
[01:38] Sara: Mostly steady for the product features — bursty for support chat. Throughput target is around 200 tokens/sec average, p95 latency goal under 350ms for single-shot generation at 512 tokens.
[01:52] Luis: Security wise — we need SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, and we have a VPC peering preference. KMS for key management is non-negotiable.
[02:05] Alex: Noted. Redwood supports SAML, has SOC2, and KMS integrations — we'll share the pack. For VPC we have Private deployments + Dedicated options. Priya, can you run through the high-level tradeoffs?
[02:18] Priya: Sure. Hosted is fastest to stand up — you call our API, we run in hosted infra. Good for quick time-to-value and small pilots. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with committed throughput, more predictable unit economics and isolation. Private is for VPC/on-prem — control plane can be customer-managed, useful where compliance or network isolation is required.
[02:38] Priya: In terms of parity, we typically onboard your model or a compatible open model and run a bench against your prompt suite. We pay attention to tokenizer differences, sampling seeds, and detokenization quirks which are the usual sources of 'weird differences'.
[02:55] Mark: For us, the main migration angle is 'exit strategy' from Azure's managed endpoint. If we go hosted we want guarantees on fallback — like if we lose parity or latency spikes, can we route back?
[03:08] Alex: Yes — we do smart routing and fallbacks. You can configure policies: prefer hosted for cost, fallback to dedicated or older model variants. Also can do A/B or canary rollouts to validate parity gradually.

[03:25] Luis: How do you handle KV cache, prefix caching — our retriever flow relies heavily on KV cache re-use and we saw vLLM caching do well locally.
[03:35] Priya: Redwood runtime supports KV cache optimizations and prefix caching. For dedicated/private we can tune cache eviction to match your session lengths. The one nuance is remote caching across nodes — there are tradeoffs, but we can instrument and show cache hit rates in the Console.
[03:51] Sara: One of our blockers is the quantization story — we have some experiments using int8 quant on vLLM to get cost down. Does Redwood support quantized weights for hosted or dedicated?
[04:03] Priya: Yes — we have quantization profiles. Hosted supports certain quantized model variants; Dedicated/Private allows more flexible quantization (including int8/int4 variants) depending on GPU architecture. We'll propose quantization options in the recommendations doc.

[04:20] [04:25] Mark: When you do parity testing, do you run against the same random seeds? Our evaluation is sensitive to sampling.
[04:33] Priya: We try to match generator configs — temperature, top_p, seeds when deterministic eval is needed. If you're using sampling in production we usually compare distribution metrics across many samples rather than exact tokens.
[04:46] Sara: For embeddings, we've seen subtle differences between model families and tokenizers that break downstream similarity thresholds. Any tooling for migration on embeddings?
[04:58] Priya: We provide per-embedding distance drift metrics and can run a mapping analysis — if embeddings drift we can suggest calibrations or recommend model variants with close embedding spaces.

[05:12] Luis: Network and egress — for Private deployments, does Redwood require us to open specific egress to a control plane, or can it be fully air-gapped?
[05:23] Alex: Private can be deployed in VPC with a customer-managed control plane; fully air-gapped on-prem packages are available for enterprise engagements but bring additional operational overhead and licensing terms. We'll include options in the pack.

[05:40] [05:47] Mark: Ok, what about bringing our custom fine-tuned models? We have a couple of checkpoints and a custom training pipeline.
[05:55] Priya: You can bring checkpoints. For hosted we usually ingest a model artifact into our catalog and run tests. For private/dedicated you can keep artifacts in your S3 or registry and mount or stage them for the runtime. We also support model version pinning and rollout policies.
[06:10] Sara: Is there a size limit or specific formats you prefer? Our checkpoints are standard pytorch but we also have some ONNX exports.
[06:18] Priya: We accept torch, HF format, and have support for ONNX in certain cases. The size limit is mostly bounded by the storage policy; for large models we recommend dedicated. We'll note the formats in the checklist.

[06:35] Luis: Can we run our TGI stack behind Redwood or replace it? We're using TGI to serve some low-latency endpoints.
[06:44] Priya: You can run Redwood in front as a unified API and route to TGI-based cluster as a backend if you want. Or you can migrate wholly to our runtime. Many customers do a hybrid phased approach to compare production behavior.
[06:56] Sara: For the eval plan, can we include tests specifically comparing vLLM local runs to Redwood hosted and Redwood dedicated? We want to see per-token cost and latency and the small prompt regression set.
[07:07] Priya: Absolutely. We'll create a benchmark template that includes vLLM, TGI, hosted Redwood, dedicated Redwood, and run sample sets. We'll need your sample keys and a small dataset — maybe 200 prompts across use cases.

[07:20] [07:25] Alex: Quick question on billing and cost — Mark, are you looking for usage-based only or committed reserved?
[07:33] Mark: Ideally reserved for predictable cost, but want the flexibility to burst. We want committed monthly throughput for our core flows.
[07:40] Alex: Dedicated fits that model — reserved GPU pools and burst options. We'll put together committed vs pay-as-you-go scenarios.

[07:50] Luis: We need to verify data residency — some PHI-adjacent telemetry can't leave region. Does Redwood offer region locking for hosted?
[07:59] Priya: Hosted can be region-aware but for strict residency we recommend Private in your VPC or Dedicated in a regional cluster. We'll flag regional options.

[08:13] Sara: Are there examples of customers who left Azure OpenAI and moved to Redwood? Any migration notes?
[08:20] Alex: We have case studies but will share redacted notes. Typical friction points are: tokenization differences, sampling config mismatches, and retraining/recalibration on embeddings. Our onboarding SEs work through those.

[08:35] [08:40] Mark: For the POC scope, what would a minimal pilot look like? Two weeks? One month?
[08:46] Priya: Minimal pilot is often 2-4 weeks: 1) onboarding and access, 2) run parity benchmarks, 3) production shadowing for a few hundred requests, 4) review. If you want production traffic we can do a canary with routing.
[09:00] Sara: Shadowing means traffic sent to both endpoints and outcomes compared?
[09:05] Priya: Yes, dual-write/dual-run to compare outputs and metrics without affecting users.

[09:18] Luis: Does Redwood expose traces and token-level cost per request? That's key for us.
[09:25] Priya: Yes Console shows token-level cost, p50/p95 latencies, per-route breakdowns, and tracing hooks. We can grant dashboard access during the pilot.

[09:38] Alex: Let's talk failure modes — model degradation/regression detection — we have quality monitoring and alerts tied to prompt sets. Priya: we can set regression thresholds and auto-roll back to previous model variant on anomaly.
[09:55] Mark: Good. How tolerant is the fallback latency when routing to a different region variant? Users will notice spikes.
[10:03] Priya: It depends on network distance; for cross-region fallback we recommend warm pools and autoscaling to mitigate cold starts. Also model variant compatibility matters — if you fallback to a smaller model responses may be shorter or different.

[10:18] Sara: A small nit — token counting alignment. We got burned once when moving between providers due to tokenization differences causing cost variance.
[10:28] Priya: We'll provide tokenization diffs and cost modeling. It's part of the migration checklist.

[10:40] [10:45] Mark: Ok let's dive a bit deeper technically — Priya, can you explain the compilation/kernel selection piece? Our infra folks were curious how you get better throughput than plain vLLM.
[10:55] Priya: Sure. Runtime picks kernels based on model shapes and hardware — we swap in optimized attention kernels, fused ops, and sequence-length-aware scheduling. It also uses continuous batching which groups low-latency requests without adding much tail latency. Combined with quantization-friendly paths, you often get lower cost than generic vLLM setups.
[11:19] Luis: When you say continuous batching, does that increase p95? We've seen batch windows that spike tail latency.
[11:26] Priya: We use adaptive batching bounded by latency SLOs; we won't hold requests beyond configured windows. For high-priority routes you can set low batching windows.
[11:36] Sara: Any limits on model token lengths or KV cache size we should be aware of?
[11:42] Priya: Limits depend on deployment type and GPU memory. We'll gather your session sizes and recommend configurations.

[11:54] [12:00] Mark: About licensing and on-prem — what does the enterprise contract look like? Support SLAs?
[12:08] Alex: For Private we do platform licensing plus support tiers; Dedicated is usually committed capacity with SLA-backed latency/uptime. We'll include a redlined MSA example and SLA summary.

[12:20] Luis: Curious about observability integrations — we use Datadog and Splunk.
[12:26] Priya: Console integrates with Datadog and can send logs to Splunk; we also provide traces and a webhook for events.

[12:38] Sara: For the bench we want to run a sweep across temp/top_p seeds and compare embedding drift — can you recommend sample sizes?
[12:46] Priya: For sampling distributions 1k prompts with multiple draws is ideal; for deterministic regression 200 curated prompts is typical. We'll propose the concrete numbers in the benchmark template.

[13:00] [13:05] Mark: Network throughput — for dedicated clusters, what's peak concurrency per GPU you typically see?
[13:12] Priya: Depends on model size. For Llama-2-13B-bit or equivalent, you can get hundreds of concurrent small requests per GPU using batching and kv cache; we'll model with your prompt length distribution.

[13:28] Luis: Regarding secrets and keys, can we integrate our HSM for signing and KMS?
[13:34] Alex: Yes HSM/KMS integrations are supported for Private and Dedicated; hosted uses our managed KMS but you can request BYOK patterns for enterprise.

[13:48] Sara: Any gotchas you've seen when teams migrate from Anthropic? They mentioned different behaviors in safety layers.
[13:55] Priya: Safety layers and prompt templates often require retuning. With Anthropic the framing is sometimes different; we help map safety policy behavior and test regressions as part of the pilot.

[14:10] [14:15] Mark: Ok — how do we measure success for the pilot? What are your recommended success criteria?
[14:22] Priya: Typical criteria: parity on 200 prompt suite (pass/fail thresholds), p95 latency under target for 1k sampled requests, embedding drift below a threshold, and cost per 1M tokens within projected delta.
[14:36] Mark: That sounds reasonable. Sara, Luis — any concerns?
[14:41] Sara: Need to ensure the test harness can run both local vLLM and Redwood endpoints — we have infra to run it but will need the benchmark template.
[14:51] Luis: I want network diagrams and clear egress endpoints before we open peering.

[15:02] Alex: We'll include those in the security pack.

[15:10] [15:16] Priya: Quick note on model variants — for some of your workflows we might recommend a different backbone open model that gives similar semantics but better latency/cost; we'll surface that as part of the recommendations.
[15:30] Mark: If we pick dedicated vs private, can we later pivot to hosted to save costs?
[15:36] Alex: Yes, the deployment abstraction lets you change routing policies; some model artifacts might need conversion but we support rollbacks and migrations.

[15:46] Sara: One more question — logs retention and PII redaction for transcripts. We need controls to redact PII from training telemetry.
[15:55] Priya: We have configurable retention and PII redaction hooks; for Private you control retention. We'll document the options.

[16:05] [16:10] Mark: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[16:13] Alex: I'll send the SOC2 pack, regional and network diagram, and a POC pricing sketch by Monday 11/10.
[16:19] Priya: I'll send the benchmark template and suggested prompt sets by 11/12.
[16:24] Sara: I'll share our sample prompts and telemetry (traces) by 11/09.
[16:27] Luis: We'll review the network diagram and get back with any restrictions.

[16:35] [16:38] Mark: Sounds good. Anything else?
[16:41] Alex: No, thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[16:45] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[16:48] Mark: Thanks all.

[56:00] End of recording
